cards.explanation: The answer is that his feet had almost stumbled. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says it plain: “But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled; my steps had nearly slipped.” He could have stopped at the nice first line and left it there. Instead he tells on himself. I respect that, friends, because most of us would have kept the wobble off the record.

The answer is envied. Asaph says, “For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.” It's that feeling when you see somebody else's vacation pictures on a Monday morning, and you're sitting at your desk. Asaph doesn't dress it up, friends. He just calls it envy.

The answer is burdens. The psalm says, “They are free of the burdens others carry; they are not afflicted like other men.” You know that coworker who never gets handed the hard assignments while everybody else's desk is buried? That's how Asaph sees them. Life's weight just seems to skip them.

The answer is that they mock and threaten. Asaph says, “They mock and speak with malice; with arrogance they threaten oppression.” Mocking, malice and threats are what he names, friends. I think that's the part that stings.
The answer is False. The verse says, “They set their mouths against the heavens, and their tongues strut across the earth.” So heaven isn't left out of their big talk, friends. It's right in it.

The answer is whether God even knows. The wicked say, “How can God know? Does the Most High have knowledge?” They're not asking anything big about being forgiven or paid back. They're wondering whether He even knows what's going on. Asaph is quoting them here, friends, he's not agreeing with them.

The answer is all for nothing. Asaph says, “Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure; in innocence I have washed my hands.” In vain means it felt like it was for nothing. He's looking at his clean hands and the wicked's easy life, and it's not adding up for him. I think we've all had a moment like that, friends.

The answer is True. Asaph says, “For I am afflicted all day long and punished every morning.” That's the hard part for him. He kept his heart pure, and mornings still feel heavy. I think this one hurts, friends.

The answer is that he'd betray God's children. Asaph says, “then I would have betrayed Your children.” He's got all these thoughts in his head, but he knows what talking that way would do. Some words are better kept in the oven until they're done, friends.

The answer is God's sanctuary. That's the turn, friends. Asaph says it was troublesome “…until I entered God’s sanctuary; then I discerned their end.” He didn't figure it out by staring harder at the problem. Something changed when he went into that place.

The answer is end. Asaph says, “then I discerned their end.” He'd been staring at where the wicked were right now. In the sanctuary he saw where they were headed. That makes a big difference, friends.
The answer is True. Asaph says, “Surely You set them on slick ground; You cast them down into ruin.” I think it looked like solid ground from the outside. Now he sees it differently, friends.

The answer is ignorant. The psalm says, “I was senseless and ignorant; I was a brute beast before You.” Asaph looks back at his grieving time and doesn't go easy on himself. That's a man being honest, friends. I think that honesty is part of why the psalm works.

The answer is False. Asaph says, “Yet I am always with You; You hold my right hand.” That little word “yet” carries a lot. He messed up in his thinking, and he's still held. Friends, that's good news for all of us.

The answer is that God guides him with His counsel. The psalm says, “You guide me with Your counsel, and later receive me in glory.” Notice what Asaph gets. It's not a pile of stuff, it's guidance. And there's more coming after that, friends.

The two words are fail and strength. Asaph says, “My flesh and my heart may fail…” He's honest that he's not made of steel. Then he gets to the good part, friends: “…but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.” A portion is what is his, and he says it's God Himself.

The answer is that it is good to draw near to God. Asaph says, “But as for me, it is good to draw near to God.” Remember, at the start he was staring at what the wicked had. Now he's looking at who he has. That's quite the turn, friends.
